Bulk-added venues are more rural (75% urban against 86% for all listed venues) and later earn a mean rating of 2.09 against 3.03. So the 0.104 is an effect for the kind of venue that waits to be added, not a cleaner estimate of the 0.052. The ladder supports "positive, and not an artifact of owner timing". It does not support a single number. Second, the estimator is part of the evidence. Ordinary two-way fixed effects give 0.054 for the bulk sample, about half the two-stage estimate. The paper explains its choice by its setting: the panel is unbalanced in calendar time, and Yelp's reach grows over the sample, so effects should differ by when a venue was listed. That is the case in which the robust estimators of @sec-causal-week06 matter. The two-way results go in an appendix, so a reader can see the gap. **Measurement is validated where it could fail.** Two of the paper's inputs are proxies, and each gets its own check. Alcohol receipts stand in for total revenue, and an appendix assembles outside evidence that the two move together. The tax-to-Yelp match comes from Yelp's internal matcher, which the authors audited with three crowdworkers per venue on 750 venues. Of the matched venues, 241 of 250 really were on Yelp. Of the unmatched venues, 202 of 250 really were absent. The second number deserves more weight than the working paper gives it. The paper says only false positives affect its regressions, but never-listed venues are its main control group. A listed venue misclassified as unlisted therefore sits among the controls, and with about one unmatched venue in five actually listed, the bias runs toward zero. **The mechanism comes from who gains, not from a mediator.** The first specimen measured a mediator, and the second decomposed the outcome. This paper takes a third route, and it is the one open to anyone without a mediator series. Each candidate mechanism predicts which venues should gain more. If a listing works by standing in for reputation the venue cannot build otherwise, gains should be larger where reputation is hard to build: independents rather than chains, and tourist areas whose customers lack local knowledge. If a listing works by revealing quality to people who would not otherwise see it, gains should be larger for better products. The published abstract reports both patterns. Independents and venues in tourist areas gain more, and so do larger venues and those with good reviews. Each split is a prediction stated before the table, so the heterogeneity table is the mechanism test. A disclosure result answers the opening puzzle. Venues that stayed off the platform until the bulk import earned lower ratings, as voluntary-disclosure models predict: owners who expect bad reviews have a reason not to list. Even so, they gained from being listed. The honesty requirement applies with full force here, because no one randomized chain status. A chain-versus-independent split is also a split by size, location, and management. Moderation evidence is consistent with a mechanism. It does not isolate one. Its strongest form, which this design reaches toward, pairs splits on which rival mechanisms predict opposite signs, so that only one story fits the whole pattern. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Explaining an effect without a model 1. Open with the descriptive fact that makes the causal question puzzling (here, free listings that many owners skip). 2. Name who chooses the treatment date, and build a ladder of samples in which someone progressively further from the outcome chooses it. 3. Read the ladder by the direction its estimates move, and say what population each rung represents. 4. Justify the estimator from features of the setting (unbalanced panel, effects that grow with the platform), and show the naive estimator in an appendix. 5. Audit every constructed variable, and work out which group each error type contaminates. 6. Derive from each candidate mechanism a prediction about who gains more, state it before the table, and treat the heterogeneity table as the mechanism test. 7. Use the selection result (who stayed out) to answer the puzzle you opened with. ::: The template transfers directly to studies of firms adopting a free digital channel, such as opening a social media account, joining a marketplace, or claiming a profile. Each shares the three problems this paper solves. The adopter picks the date, the non-adopters are a selected group worth describing in their own right, and the outcome has to come from outside the platform, or the effect of being on the platform is measured with the platform's own data. The rung to look for is an adoption whose date someone other than the firm set. Tax receipts, permits, and other administrative records solve the outcome problem when they exist, and @sec-data-txmb shows what one such source takes to use. ### A Fourth Specimen: A Small Reward Framed as Four Open Questions {#sec-sw-emb-plasma} @bruers2026plasma, published online in *Management Science* in 2026, is about as plain as a field experiment gets. For this model the dissertation reports 3.3% and 5.5%, fitted with autocorrelated errors that we did not reproduce. Its preferred donor-level fixed-effects Poisson model gives 4.6% and 7.1%, the figures the published abstract carries. The figure also shows why the donor-level model carries the paper. With four centers per arm, the pre-period ratios wander by up to about five percent either side of 1. Month 0, before any treatment, already sits near 1.06 in both arms. The late spike in month 13 comes from a recruitment campaign, which the dissertation notes worked best at the two largest centers, both in treated arms. **Substitution is priced, not just reported.** The partner collects blood and plasma at the same sites, so the experiment can see what the coupon costs in the prosocial act it did not reward. In the dissertation's numbers, the blood decline is barely significant at the donor level (p = 0.047) and not significant in the center-level model. It accounts for about one sixth of the plasma gain. The paper reports it anyway, and the cost arithmetic shows why. Every plasma donor gets the extra coupon, including those who would have come anyway. The dissertation therefore puts the marginal cost at €1.50 × 107% / 7%, about €23 per extra plasma donation, and €34 once the lost blood donations are netted out. The same dissertation's meta-analysis puts the cost of cash or vouchers worth €5 to €15 per blood donation at €20 to €120 per extra donation. A cost per net extra donation is the number a collector can act on. **The partner shapes the design, and the paper says how.** The Red Cross funded the study and supplied administrative records on 77,646 donors who gave at a center at least once over the two years. The outcome is therefore a count of donations, not a stated intention. The partner's rules also set the design's limits. An informal cap of about €5 on rewards for voluntary, unpaid donation limited the reward to three coupons. A rule against treating donors at the same center differently meant that centers, not donors, were randomized. The twelve centers were grouped by cluster analysis into four triplets of similar size and donor mix, and one center per triplet went to each arm. Matching helps, but twelve units cannot balance everything: 43% of control-arm donors lived more than 15 km from their center, against 26% in each treated arm. Inference is the other cost. The dissertation clusters standard errors by donor, although treatment varies by center. With twelve clusters, a referee will ask for center-level inference such as the wild cluster bootstrap (@sec-causal-week05). Say in the paper what the partner allowed and what it cost. **Registration, described accurately.** The trial appears in the AEA RCT Registry [@bruers2024registry], but the entry was submitted in August 2024, more than a year after the intervention ended in June 2023. The dissertation states that no preregistration was done, while noting that the models and hypotheses were fixed before data collection. A registration filed after the data exist documents a design. It does not constrain the analysis the way a pre-analysis plan does, and a careful reader will check the dates. Describe your own registration by its date. **A mechanism stage without a model.** The dissertation closed by asking whether a larger reward works through donors' self-interest or by signaling that donations are more urgently needed. The published version answers with survey evidence. Small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts that call for reciprocity, and the authors suggest the findings may carry over to volunteering. The survey's design is not described in the versions we could read. Asking recipients how they interpret an incentive is a cheap mechanism stage, and the honesty requirement applies to it in full: stated interpretations are consistent with a mechanism but do not isolate one. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Making a small field experiment publishable 1. Turn the one effect into several open questions, and give each a design feature that answers it. 2. Write each question so that either answer is a result, including a null. 3. Run the panel long enough to see build-up, decay, and what happens after the treatment ends, and report effects month by month. 4. Measure the behavior the incentive might pull people away from, and fold the loss into the cost per unit gained. 5. Give reminding people of what they already get its own arm, separate from giving them more. 6. Use the partner's administrative outcomes, and state which of the partner's rules shaped the design. 7. Match inference to the unit of randomization, and say how many clusters you have. 8. Date your registration honestly, and add a direct check on mechanism, even a survey, before a referee asks for one. ::: The template carries over to loyalty programs and promotions. A points bonus on one product line is the same experiment, and substitution away from the other lines is the outcome that keeps the estimate honest. ### A Fifth Specimen: One Effect, Several Routes {#sec-sw-emb-roads} @agarwal2026road, published in *Management Science* in 2026 (finance department), ask whether building a rural road brings a village's households into the stock market. The treatment and the outcome sit far apart, and a reader's first reaction is to ask how asphalt could open a brokerage account. That distance is why the paper is useful here. The main effect takes one table. Most of the paper is spent on the routes from road to trade, and each route gets its own prediction, its own data source, and its own test. The earlier specimens each explained an effect one way: a mediator, a decomposition, a moderator table, a survey. This one runs several explanations side by side and tries to discriminate among them. The account below is drawn from the February 2022 working paper [@agarwal2022roadwp], because the published text was not accessible when this section was written. Where the published abstract differs, the difference is noted. Magnitudes need particular care. The February 2022 draft reports that a new road raises the number of new investors in a postal code by 28.7% and their trades by 64.5%. The abstract on record for the SSRN version reports 6.8% and 7.9%, and the published abstract reports no magnitude. The numbers below are the 2022 draft's and show the pattern of the argument. Take magnitudes from the published tables before quoting any. **The setting supplies the design, and the paper borrows it openly.** India's rural road program (PMGSY) built all-weather feeder roads to more than 115,000 previously unconnected villages. Development economists had already used the program to study schooling, labor, and lending, and the paper says it follows the empirical strategy of one of those studies. The new ingredient is the outcome: every trade on the National Stock Exchange by 13.5 million individual investors, each tagged with a postal code. The authors assign villages to postal codes within five kilometers, keep the 4,154 postal codes that received their first program road between October 2004 and February 2015, and estimate a monthly panel with postal-code, month, and district-by-year fixed effects. Every unit is eventually treated, so the comparison is only ever about timing (@sec-causal-did discusses what that costs). A new outcome on an accepted design is a legitimate contribution, and it leaves the referee's attention for the mechanism sections, which is where this paper wants it. **The main effect is split once before any mechanism is discussed.** New investors, defined as accounts less than three years old, drive most of the response. In the 2022 draft the effect is about six additional new investors and 214 additional trades per postal code per month, in a sample where the average postal code has 36 active investors. Effects are larger in rural postal codes and in areas of intermediate development. The poorest tenth by consumption shows no extra response relative to developed areas. That split is a boundary result and a first hint about mechanism. It is what one would expect if a road cannot create investors where there is little to invest. **Each route is written as a prediction about something other than the headline outcome.** @fig-sw-roads-routes and @tbl-sw-roads-routes give the structure. The information route says a road lowers the cost of learning about stocks, through better access to facts about companies and through more contact with people who already invest [@hong2004social]. If so, three things should follow, and none of them is the participation count. Remote places, where information was scarcest, should respond more. Portfolios should broaden. Holdings should reach toward firms farther away. The financial-inclusion route says a road brings bank branches, and a branch is where an account gets opened and where savings sit before they move. If so, the effect should concentrate in postal codes where a branch opened after the road, and money should leave savings deposits and consumption. A third candidate is a rival more than a route: roads raise incomes, and richer households buy stocks. If that were the whole story, the response should concentrate in months of good rainfall, the standard proxy for a positive income shock in rural India. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-sw-roads-routes %%| fig-cap: "The argument structure of the road-construction paper, reconstructed from the February 2022 working paper. Mechanism sections in student drafts usually re-cut the main regression by variables already in the file. Here each claim about a route is checked against a measurement that the main result did not use, which is why seven rows read as seven pieces of evidence and not one result shown seven ways. **The best split is the one on which two stories disagree.** A branch could raise participation because households want to invest and now can, or because bank staff sell investments. The authors argue that state-owned banks reach further into rural areas but earn less fee income, and so have less reason to push stock trading. The demand story therefore predicts a stronger effect for state-owned branches, and the sales story a weaker one. The estimate is stronger for state-owned branches. This is the move the third specimen reached toward: a moderator chosen because rival accounts predict opposite signs. The published abstract adds a route the 2022 draft lacks, risk sharing, under which roads should matter more where incomes are volatile, and reports limited evidence for it. A route that was proposed, tested, and found weak is reported as such, and it makes the two surviving routes more credible. **The last stage qualifies the headline.** Participation is usually treated as a good outcome, and the paper could have stopped there. It asks instead how the new investors did. In the 2022 draft, trades after road completion earn money over 1-day and 10-day holding periods, show no detectable profit over 25 days, and lose money over 140 trading days, and trading shifts toward more volatile stocks. The published abstract keeps the conclusion: infrastructure raises participation but not necessarily the quality of investment outcomes. This is a fourth stage beyond effect, mechanism, and boundary, and it changes the policy sentence. Without it the paper recommends roads as financial-inclusion policy. With it the paper says roads bring people in and something else has to help them invest well. **Where the specimen is thin.** The honesty requirement of @sec-sw-emb applies, and a conference discussion of the working paper states the problem compactly [@hong2022roaddiscussion]. A road moves everything at once: information, bank access, and income. If bank branches were treated as the variable of interest and the road as its instrument, the exclusion restriction would fail, because the road also works through the other routes. The branch split has a second weakness. A branch that opens after the road is itself an outcome of the road, and banks choose where to open, so the postal codes with new branches may be the ones where demand for investing was about to rise anyway. The discussion asks which way causation runs between branches and participation. The rainfall test addresses transitory income only, and a permanent rise in income from better market access remains a live alternative. The evidence supports "both routes are operating" and does not support a share for each. A paper that needs shares has to write down a model, as in @sec-sw-measure-model, or find separate variation in each route. The same discussion suggests a different frame, the unplanned benefits of public-goods spending, which shows that the frame was a choice. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Explaining one effect through several routes 1. Before any mechanism test, split the main effect on the margin that matters (here, new against experienced investors) so the reader knows whose behavior needs explaining. 2. Write each route as a causal sentence, then derive an implication for a variable other than the headline outcome. 3. Bring a new measurement to each implication. Re-cutting the main regression by variables already in the file is weaker evidence. 4. Include the dull rival (people simply got richer) and give it a test of its own. 5. Look for one split on which two versions of a route predict opposite signs. 6. Report a route that found little support. It makes the others more credible. 7. Say that the tests show which routes operate and do not apportion the effect among them, and flag any split that conditions on something the treatment itself caused. 8. End by asking whether the outcome you raised was good for the people concerned, and let the answer change the policy sentence. ::: The template carries over to marketing questions where a distant cause is suspected of moving a consumer outcome: broadband rollout and online shopping, a new store format and category entry, a payment technology and spending. In each, the main effect is the short part of the paper, and the list of routes, with one outside dataset apiece, is the plan for the rest. For the first of these, @sec-causal-iv-broadband lists published broadband studies by outcome and by source of variation, which is a quick way to see which routes have already been tested. ## The Lifecycle Paper: How Response Changes Across Stages {#sec-sw-lifecycle} Many marketing questions are really about a process. A product is announced, launched, reviewed, discounted, and retired. An event is advertised, held, and then sold as a recording. A customer searches, buys, uses, and complains. A lifecycle paper takes one response parameter, such as a price elasticity, an advertising effect, or the weight of word of mouth, and asks how it changes from stage to stage. The finding is the profile across stages, not a single number. Done well, the paper also says why the profile has that shape. The two usual reasons are that different people act at different stages, and that the same people know or want different things at different stages. Separating them is the core analytical task of the genre. The genre borrows from its neighbors. Each stage needs a credible estimate, as in @sec-sw-emb. The gap between stages is decomposed into selection and within-person change, as in @sec-sw-decomposition. The mechanism is often tested by moderation, as in @sec-sw-emb-listings. What sets it apart is the axis everything is organized on: a sequence of stages whose boundaries are fixed by an institution rather than by the analyst. **The specimen.** @cong2026livestream ask how demand for paid livestreams responds to price before the stream and after it, when the recording is on sale (@sec-price-lifecycle has the substance). On a Chinese knowledge-sharing platform, 2,299 talks sold at a price fixed for their whole life. Demand before the stream has an elasticity of about $-1.2$, and demand for the recording about $-0.8$. The paper traces the gap partly to who buys early (heavy users, who are more price-sensitive) and partly to what buyers know (quality is uncertain until the ratings arrive), and ends with stage-specific prices. The analyst did not choose them after looking at the data. The paper's first figure is the lifecycle itself, and the data section says what stays constant across stages. The price cannot change after listing, which is what makes a comparison of elasticities across stages meaningful. Events the platform discounted partway through are dropped for the same reason. The outcome windows (30 days on each side) are set so that stages are comparable across events, and the paper reports that they capture 85% of sales, so a reader can judge what was left out. **Test the gap, not two separate estimates.** The main specification pools both stages and interacts price with a post-stream indicator, so the difference in elasticities has its own standard error. Separate regressions for each stage appear only as a robustness check. The authors justify this in a footnote, and it is worth copying. Note also what the pooled form buys for identification. If an omitted creator quality shifts demand equally in both stages, it biases the two elasticities by the same amount and leaves the gap unbiased. Saying this out loud tells a referee which claim is the robust one. **Describe who acts in each stage before modeling why.** The first mechanism table is plain description: buyers before the stream have written more answers and have more followers than buyers of the recording. Only then does the paper estimate elasticities by buyer type. The order matters, because a selection story that has not first been shown in the raw composition reads as speculation. **Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change.** The two explanations make different predictions. If the gap is pure selection, it vanishes once buyer type is held fixed. If buyers' information changes, the gap survives within type. The paper runs this test twice: within engagement groups, and on the buyers who purchased in both stages, a group that holds composition fixed by construction. The gap survives both. A coarse proxy for type leaves some selection inside each group, so the within-type gap is an upper bound on within-buyer change. The simulation below shows why the test works. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) J <- 2000 # events, each sold before and after the stream lp <- rnorm(J, log(20), 0.6) # log price (RMB); fixed for the event's whole life xi <- rnorm(J, 0, 0.5) # event appeal, independent of price here eta <- c(frequent = 1.6, infrequent = 0.6) # each type's price sensitivity # Demand for event j in stage s from consumer type k is Poisson with mean # scale * share(k, s) * exp(xi_j - Frequent, price-sensitive users simply make up 80% of the early market and 20% of the late one. The aggregate data still show demand that is far more elastic before the event (about $-1.4$) than after it (about $-0.8$), close to the pattern in the paper. Only the split by type gives it away: within each type the gap is zero. In the second row, the buyer mix is constant and every buyer becomes less price-sensitive once quality is known, so the gap appears both in aggregate and within each type. In the third row, both are at work and the aggregate gap is roughly their sum, while the within-type gap recovers the uncertainty part alone. This is the logic of the paper's Table 10. The aggregate gap cannot tell the stories apart; the within-type gap can. **Test the within mechanism by where it should be weak.** Quality uncertainty predicts a smaller gap wherever buyers already knew what they were getting: creators with a quality badge, "hard" topics whose quality can be judged from a description, and buyers who already followed the creator. Each prediction is stated before its table, and each holds. As in @sec-sw-emb-listings, moderation is consistent with the mechanism without isolating it, and the paper concedes that live and recorded content differ in other ways too. **Check that the boundary is not an artifact of the display.** Platforms often show each stage differently. Here upcoming events sit at the top of the page and past events drift down it. If position drove the gap, elasticities would trend within each stage. Instead they are flat on both sides with a jump at the stream. The paper says plainly that it cannot rule out higher search costs for archived events. Naming the alternative you cannot exclude costs less credibility than letting a referee name it. **End with a policy and the assumption it rests on.** The counterfactual compares one price for the whole life with a price for each stage, under linear demand and independent stages. The authors call the second assumption "admittedly strong" and name the dependence it ignores (cheap early tickets could cannibalize the recording or signal quality to its buyers). A lifecycle counterfactual almost always rests on some assumption about how stages are linked, so state it and say which way relaxing it would move the answer. **A lesson from the version history.** The first public version (arXiv, July 2021) was titled "The Role of 'Live' in Livestreaming Markets." It estimated a daily elasticity curve from two weeks before to two weeks after the stream with a generalized orthogonal random forest. Elasticity was about $-0.5$ two weeks out, near zero on the stream day, and about $-0.1$ afterward, and the paper attributed the stream-day pattern to the chance to interact with the creator in real time. The published paper (June 2026 arXiv) is plainer and stronger. The question became how demand changes across the lifecycle rather than what "live" is worth. The daily curve became a two-stage contrast with a pooled test and an instrument. The real-time interaction mechanism was dropped, because weekly elasticities in the run-up to the stream turned out to be flat. A self-selection mechanism and a pricing counterfactual were added. Coarser stages identified cleanly made a better paper than a fine-grained curve identified by a flexible method, and the mechanism the data no longer supported was cut rather than kept. **The genre in this book.** Many papers already cited here have the same shape, and reading them as one genre makes the moves easier to see. - @elberse2003 model movies released in sequence across countries, where performance in the first market shapes demand and screen allocation in later ones. - @weinberg2000salesthrough treat theatrical release and video as sequential channels and ask when the second stage should open, given that it cannibalizes the first. - @moe2002 use advance purchase orders, the pre-release stage, to forecast sales after launch. - @liu2006wordmouth trace movie word of mouth from before release through the run and ask which features of it predict box office at each point. - @eliashberg2000 build a decision-support model for evaluating a movie before release. - @golder2004 explain the turning points of the product life cycle (takeoff and slowdown) with informational cascades. - @deighton2012addingbricks show that the effect of opening stores on a retailer's catalog and online channels changes with time since opening. - @lemon2016 organize customer experience into pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase stages, the conceptual frame for journey papers. - @colicev2019 link firm and user content to separate stages of the marketing funnel. - @kim2026customization ask whether a first customization experience changes the later stages of a customer's journey, and separate who customizes from what customizing does with a randomized experience manipulation (@sec-causal-born-or-made). - @xie2001advance give the theory for the stage before consumption, when buyers are uncertain about their own future state. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for writing your own lifecycle paper 1. Define the stages by an event that changes what buyers know or who is buying (announcement, release, first reviews, the event itself, expiry), not by calendar time. Draw the lifecycle as the paper's first figure. 2. State what is held constant across stages (price, product, display) and drop units where the firm intervened partway through. 3. Choose windows that make stages comparable across units, and report how much of total activity they capture. 4. Estimate one pooled model with stage interactions so the gap has a standard error, and keep separate per-stage regressions as robustness. 5. Identify the level of the parameter in every stage; then say which confounds the pooled form differences out of the gap. 6. Show who acts in each stage with descriptive tables before proposing any mechanism. 7. Split the gap into selection and within-buyer change: estimate by buyer type, and on buyers active in more than one stage. Report how much of the gap survives. 8. For each within-buyer mechanism, name the units where it should be weak, state the prediction before the table, and test it. 9. Check whether the stage boundary is an artifact of how the platform presents each stage: look for a jump at the boundary rather than a trend within stages. 10. Turn the gap into a stage-specific policy, write down the assumption that links the stages (cannibalization, signaling, strategic waiting), and say which way relaxing it would move the answer. 11. Bound the claim: one platform, one kind of content, one period. ::: ## The Field-Experiment Paper from an Emerging Market {#sec-sw-emerging-field} A growing share of the data that marketing students hold comes from markets the field's journals rarely see: a panel of retailers in Vietnam, a survey of vendors in Lagos, transaction logs from a network of mobile-money agents. Writing a paper from such data runs into a problem that none of the templates above solves on its own. The paper usually offers no new theory and no new method. Its evidence does not come as a list of hypotheses, each confirmed by a coefficient. What it has instead is a setting where an important question can be answered cleanly, and a design that answers it. Turning that into a paper takes craft. @anderson2026datadecisions, published online in *Marketing Science* in October 2026, is a well-built specimen. It is a close cousin of the effect–mechanism–boundary paper (@sec-sw-emb): a randomized experiment supplies the effect, and measured intermediate outcomes carry the mechanism. (The published article was not accessible when this section was written. The publisher deposits a one-sentence abstract with Crossref. The fuller sources are the abstract of a 2022 working paper in the Private Enterprise Development in Low-Income Countries (PEDL) series, the abstract of a 2023 SSRN version, the trial's entry in the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0005591), the article's deposited reference list, and Chicago Booth Review coverage, including a 2024 article and a 2026 podcast interview with Chintagunta [@chicagobooth2024apps; @chicagobooth2026podcast]. Each number below names the version it comes from. Where versions disagree, the text says so. The section structure discussed here is a reconstruction of what a paper in this genre must contain, not the article's table of contents.) ### The study in two paragraphs The authors randomized 550 growth-oriented micro and small enterprises in Rwanda into three arms (registry). Two hundred fifty treatment firms received an Android smartphone, a data plan, and MARKETmanager, an app the researchers designed. Owners used it to record sales, products, customers, and marketing actions, and it returned monthly reports comparing the firm's current performance with its past. Fifty placebo firms received the phone and data plan without the app. Two hundred fifty control firms received nothing during the study and were promised access afterward. The registry dates the intervention from July 2019 to March 2020. The 2022 working paper describes nine months of treatment, and the 2024 Booth Review article seven, ending as COVID-19 arrived. Staff visited treated owners to help them enter and read the data: weekly according to the registry, monthly according to the 2024 article. That article adds that the visitors explained the reports but gave no advice on what to do with them. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the visitors as mostly undergraduates chosen for their lack of business experience. The findings come in four families, listed in the same order in every version of the abstract. Usage started low and rose by the third month. The 2022 abstract reports daily usage rates of 90–95%. The 2024 article reports that about 30% of treated firms used the app daily at first, rising to 60%. The two figures probably measure different things, and only the paper can settle which. On mental performance, "objective ability and psychological tests" (six of them, according to the 2024 article) show gains in reasoning, memory, logic, and calculation. On practices, treated firms adopted product-management activities, with spillovers into accounting practices the app never targeted. On money, monthly sales were 36.4% and monthly profits 29.2% higher than in the control group on average. These two figures appear in the 2022, 2023, and published abstracts. The published abstract adds that comparisons with the placebo arm, which holds phone and internet access fixed, attribute the gains to the analytics rather than the device. ### Where the contribution comes from without a new theory or method A paper like this does not claim to have invented anything. Its contribution is one, or several, of three other kinds, and the specimen makes all three. 1. *A causal estimate of a quantity people already act on.* Governments, donors, and software vendors already sell analytics to small firms on the assumption that it pays. The gap is not a missing theory but a missing number. The 2023 abstract says so in one line: analytics is "widely promoted", but evidence on its effects for individual entrepreneurs "remains limited". An evidence gap of this kind is legitimate when the quantity is policy-relevant and nobody has randomized it. 2. *A mechanism measured, not asserted.* "Analytics improves decisions" is usually an assumption. Here it becomes an observation, because the authors tested the owners themselves. A battery of cognitive tests is a measurement contribution in a marketing journal, and it turns a firm-level result into a claim about people. 3. *A tension resolved.* The 2022 abstract opens with two literatures that predict opposite signs. In one, technology builds the user's human capital. In the other, analysis paralysis, confirmation bias, information overload, and "brain drain" erode it. The deposited reference list covers both: studies of cognitive training and neuroplasticity on one side, and on the other a 2025 experiment in which generative AI without guardrails harmed high-school students' learning. A two-sided prior is what makes an empirical answer a contribution (@sec-sw-open-question). Neither side could have called the result in advance. The contribution sentence of @sec-sw-contribution adapts accordingly. It becomes: "We estimate the effect of [a treatment decision makers already buy or fund] on [the outcomes they care about] among [a population described by its economic role], a quantity prior work could not estimate because [the treatment is everywhere where data are rich, or nobody randomized it], and we show that the effect runs through [measured intermediate outcomes]." The title history shows the same move. The 2022 working paper asked a question: "Is (Smart) Technology Really Making Us Dumber?" The 2023 SSRN version answered it: "(Smart) Technology Doesn't Make Us Dumber". The published title drops the provocation altogether: "From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market". It names the causal chain in order and puts the setting last, as a scope condition. The country does not appear in it at all. ### The country as the source of variation, not a curiosity The hardest sentence in an emerging-market paper answers the question a referee in Chicago or Rotterdam is silently asking: why should I care about Rwanda? The weak answer describes the country. The strong answer says what the country makes estimable. In rich markets almost every firm already has some data, so the value of analytics cannot be estimated from a starting point of none. In the specimen's setting, few micro and small enterprises "formally record their marketing data" (registry). In the podcast, Chintagunta puts the baseline share with any records at about 30%. The setting is where the treatment can be switched on from zero. Write the setting paragraph as an argument about variation, and the reader stops treating the country as exotic. The second move puts the reader's own literature beside the result. @bargill2024ebay randomized eBay's Seller Hub, a data-rich seller dashboard, and found that access raised sellers' revenues by 3.6% on average. The same question in a rich platform setting produced an effect about a tenth the size. The outcomes, populations, and measurement all differ, so the comparison is a hypothesis about where analytics pays most, not an estimate. Stated that way, it gives a US reader a reason to care: your number is small because your firms already know what this treatment teaches. The third move describes the firms by their economic role, not their geography. Most are retail shops, with some services such as hair salons (podcast). The registry frames them as the last mile through which large companies reach consumers in emerging markets. A brand manager at a consumer-goods firm recognizes that population at once. The fourth move is a research program. The same team has varied the marketing lever while holding the population type fixed. Marketing versus finance training came first in South Africa [@anderson2018], then volunteer marketers in Uganda [@anderson2021marketersmatter], customer-feedback seeking in Rwanda [@kaul2025callmemaybe], and now analytics. The Uganda paper appeared in the *Journal of Marketing* issue on better marketing for a better world, whose editorial invites work of this kind [@chandy2021better]. Each paper inherits the credibility of the last one's fieldwork. A student with one emerging-market dataset should ask early which second paper the same population and instruments could support. Two habits of style follow. Name the country in the setting section, not in the headline claim. And give the real reason for the choice of country alongside the scientific one. Chintagunta says plainly in the podcast that the study went to Rwanda partly because the research funding was there. Chintagunta also cites the country's push on technology access and its heavy use of mobile payments. A paper can state both. It should not claim the country was picked for representativeness unless it was. ### Evidence without hypothesis tests: the design is the argument The specimen has no H1 through H4. In their place it has a design whose arms define the estimands, and outcome families reported in causal order. The table below reconstructs the estimands from the registry's design. | Contrast | What it estimates | What a writer must say about it | |---|---|---| | Treatment vs. control | The whole bundle: phone, data, app, and support visits | This is the policy-relevant effect of offering the program | | Treatment vs. placebo | The app and its support, holding phone and internet fixed | It answers "it's just the smartphone", but the placebo arm has only 50 firms, so the contrast is less precise | | Placebo vs. control | Phone and data alone | A useful null if it is small, and a finding in its own right if not | : The estimands implied by a three-arm design with a placebo, reconstructed from the registry entry for @anderson2026datadecisions. {#tbl-sw-emerging-estimands} Several practices then replace hypothesis-by-hypothesis testing. - *Report outcome families in causal order.* Usage, then mind, then practices, then money. Each family is reported as an effect with a confidence interval, not as a verdict on a hypothesis. The order is the story: a reader who has seen take-up and cognition is ready to believe the sales figure. - *Separate the offer from the use.* With usage low at first, the intent-to-treat effect answers the policy question of what offering the app does. Scaling by usage (treatment on the treated) answers how much using it does. Report both, and say which one the abstract quotes. The public versions do not say which estimate the 36.4% is. - *Be exact about registration.* The trial was registered on March 24, 2020, after the intervention began in July 2019, and no analysis plan appears on the public page. A writer in that position should say "registered" and not "pre-registered", should name the primary outcomes (here sales and profits), and should label everything else as secondary or exploratory. Readers forgive late registration far more readily than a claim that turns out to be false. - *Control multiplicity by family.* Six cognitive tests and a list of practice items invite fishing. The standard remedy is a summary index per family, with p-values adjusted across families [@anderson2008multiple]. That paper is in the specimen's reference list, which suggests, though the public versions cannot confirm it, that the authors use this approach. - *Show the mechanism through intermediate outcomes, and say what that cannot prove.* The reference list includes the causal-mediation framework of @imai2010general. Cognition and practices were not themselves randomized, so a mediation estimate rests on sequential ignorability (@sec-causal-mediation-assumptions). The safe claim is that the effect on intermediate outcomes and the effect on profits line up as the mechanism predicts. The placebo arm strengthens that claim, but it cannot turn it into an experiment on the mediator. - *Treat heterogeneity as a test of mechanism, not a search.* The reference list includes generalized random forests, debiased machine learning for conditional average treatment effects, and lasso-based selection of controls, the current toolkit for heterogeneity in experiments. Use the forest for discovery and label it that way. Separately, name two or three subgroups that the mechanism says should gain more, such as owners with weak baseline numeracy if the mechanism runs through calculation skill. In the podcast, Chintagunta says that the owners who already kept records showed directionally similar gains but were too few to test. Writing that sentence is the honest version of a heterogeneity result. - *Benchmark the magnitude.* A 29.2% profit gain means little until it is compared with something. The 2024 Booth Review article reports the authors' cost calculation: about \$4–\$6 a month in variable cost, an unsubsidized up-front cost of \$170–\$210 per business, and break-even in roughly 7–10 months. Set that against the alternatives a funder would consider. The same team's volunteer marketers raised monthly profits by 35.8% in Uganda [@anderson2021marketersmatter]. Classroom training has a mixed record, which @mckenzie2021training reassesses. Intensive consulting worked for large Indian textile plants but at a much higher cost per firm [@bloom2013management]. Express the effect as a percentage of the control mean, in local currency and in dollars at a stated exchange rate, and per dollar spent. ### The institutional section as persuasion In a paper from an unfamiliar market, the setting and intervention sections do work that a literature review does elsewhere. They make the reader trust a design they cannot picture. Four kinds of detail carry most of the weight. - *Who the firms are.* Sector mix, size, how they were recruited, what "growth-oriented" meant as a screening rule, and how the sample compares with a national benchmark. The specimen's reference list includes Rwanda's 2020 Establishment Census, the natural benchmark for that comparison. - *What the treatment was, screen by screen.* What owners entered and how often, what came back, and what the visitors were and were not allowed to say. The podcast gives the level of detail a reader needs. Owners entered whether the shop was open and its revenue each day. Every two weeks they entered their top three products with price and cost, from which the app computed margins, together with counts of regular, occasional, and new customers. Detail of this kind is persuasive because it rules out the most damaging alternative, that the program was really free consulting. Visitors chosen for their lack of business experience serve the same purpose. - *What everyone else received.* Placebo firms had their data plans topped up, and every arm had enumerator visits (podcast). Balanced contact is the main answer to Hawthorne effects and experimenter demand, and it belongs in the design section, not in a footnote. - *How the design changed.* An earlier PEDL-funded project by the same team, active 2016–2018, describes a larger plan on its public page: 1,500 owners around Kigali, a finance-information tool and a marketing-information tool in separate arms, and follow-ups at 12 and 18–24 months. The public record does not say whether the executed study is a revision of that plan. A referee who finds such a page will ask. One paragraph explaining what changed and why pre-empts the question. ### Would it work elsewhere? The external-validity paragraph is where emerging-market papers most often say too much or too little. The productive form names the conditions under which the effect should travel, not a list of countries. For the specimen those conditions are plausibly three: owners do not already track their key numbers, the owner makes the decisions, and the phone and data cost little relative to monthly profit. Each condition can be checked against another market's data. Chintagunta declines to extrapolate to US corner stores, saying such a claim would be "anecdotal" (podcast). That restraint is a model to copy. Two further caveats belong in the paragraph. The sample was screened for growth orientation, so the estimate describes firms that pass that screen, not the median microenterprise. And persistence is a separate question. The 2024 article reports a March 2021 follow-up of 14 randomly chosen treated owners, 13 of whom still kept records. Evidence that thin is useful as illustration and should be labeled as such, not counted as a long-run estimate. ### Credible numbers where firms keep no books The specimen's measurement problem is general to the genre, and in one respect it is sharper. The published abstract says treated firms "report" higher sales and profits, and the verb matters: in settings without books, outcomes are self-reported. Here the treatment is record-keeping, so it changes the instrument that measures the outcome. Treated owners may report more accurately, or more optimistically, than control owners who are guessing. The defenses a referee will look for are these: 1. Measure outcomes with the same enumerator protocol in every arm. Never use the app's own records as the outcome for treated firms, because control firms have no such records. 2. Collect several follow-up rounds and average them. Noisy outcomes like microenterprise profits gain more power from repeated measurement than from extra firms [@mckenzie2012moret], a paper the specimen cites. 3. Cross-check reported profit against reported sales minus reported costs, and state the trimming or winsorizing rule before looking at treatment effects. 4. Pair self-reports with outcomes that are hard to inflate. Business practices measured as a standard index of yes/no items [@mckenzie2017practices] and objective cognitive tests both qualify. In the podcast, Chintagunta describes the Cognitive Reflection Test [@frederick2005crt], with about 0.7 of three items correct in the control group against about one in the treatment group. These are oral, approximate figures. The exact estimates are in the paper. 5. Ask whether a test measures the trained skill or general ability. An owner who computes margins every two weeks has practiced arithmetic. A gain on a calculation test is near transfer. A gain on reasoning or memory tests is the more surprising claim and needs the stronger defense. The specimen's reference list includes the cognitive-training literature in which this distinction is argued. 6. Report attrition by arm and bound the estimates for it. The public versions give no attrition figures. The study ended as COVID-19 arrived, which makes the timing of the endline survey and the response rate worth a paragraph of their own. 7. Account for local shocks. The reference list includes spatially robust standard errors and satellite night-lights data, which suggests the authors treat local economic conditions explicitly. That is worth doing whenever firms cluster in a few markets. ### The anatomy of the genre | Section | Rhetorical job | What the specimen supplies (version) | |---|---|---| | Title | Name the causal chain;
