Most of the template still applies. The country is still a source of variation, the institutional section still has to make a design believable, the outcome families can still be ordered as a chain, and the measurement defenses apply unchanged. What changes is the design paragraph. The arms that define the estimands become an identification argument: a policy rollout, a boundary, or a staggered adoption whose timing the firm did not choose. Those arguments are developed in @sec-sw-emb-listings and @sec-causal-inference. If no such argument is available, the honest genre is the descriptive paper (@sec-sw-descriptive), whose contribution is a pattern that nobody had documented, stated with its own ceiling. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for writing your own emerging-market paper 1. Write the setting paragraph as an argument about variation: say what the country lets you estimate that a rich-data market cannot. 2. Put the closest result from a high-income setting beside yours, and explain the difference in magnitude as a hypothesis rather than a finding. 3. Describe the firms by their economic role (retailers, suppliers, agents) and benchmark the sample against a national census or survey. 4. State the contribution as an estimate, a measured mechanism, or a resolved tension, and name the decision maker who needs the number. 5. Let the arms or the identifying variation define the estimands, and include a placebo or comparison that answers the most obvious objection. 6. Report outcome families in causal order, one index per family, with multiplicity adjusted across families. 7. Give both the effect of the offer and the effect of use, and say which one the abstract quotes. 8. Say exactly when the study was registered and what was pre-specified. 9. Present mechanisms through intermediate outcomes, and state the assumption that a mediation estimate needs. 10. Name the subgroups the mechanism predicts before running exploratory heterogeneity, and report underpowered subgroups as underpowered. 11. Measure outcomes with one protocol across arms, average several rounds, and pair self-reports with measures that are hard to inflate. 12. Cost the intervention and compare it per dollar with the alternatives a funder would consider. 13. Write the external-validity paragraph as a list of conditions, and label thin follow-up evidence as illustration. 14. Give the real reason the study ran where it did, alongside the scientific one. ::: ## The Design-Science Method Paper {#sec-sw-design-science} The methods paper sketched under paper types has a codified variant in information systems that marketing scholars increasingly write for, review for, and borrow from: the computational design-science paper. Its artifact is a method, usually a predictive model, and its contribution is design knowledge, meaning a statement of which design choices solve which problem and why [@hevner2004design; @gregor2013positioning; @abbasi2024pathways]. Students who know only the hypothesis-testing template find these papers hard to imitate, because the logic that holds them together is never stated in any one place. The paper reveals it through a handful of tables. Two papers from the same September 2026 issue of *Information Systems Research* serve as specimens. @wang2026drdl propose DRDL, a deep-learning method that predicts whether and when a firm will fall into financial distress from several data sources at once (@sec-mmf-drdl reimplements it). @xu2026upstar propose UPSTAR, a product recommender that first infers *why* a customer bought each item, out of stable preference or exploratory intent, and then predicts the next purchase. The domains share almost nothing, but the architecture is the same, and the shared architecture is what to learn. (DRDL was read in full. For UPSTAR, only the published abstract and the authors' released code were accessible when this section was written, so statements about UPSTAR's internals come from the code.) ### The spine: one artifact per challenge The single most important object in a design-science paper is a table that most readers skim: the design framework. It runs from goals to challenges to design components, and it is built backward from the problem's own features. DRDL's version (their Table 2) has two goals, five challenges, and five components, one component for each challenge. | Paper | Goal | Challenge | Design component | |---|---|---|---| | DRDL | Use entangled multiview data | Separate complementary from redundant signal | Discrete multiview recoder | | | | Fuse views without carrying redundancy | Mask-based view fusion decoder | | | Predict risk over several horizons | Risk must not fall as the horizon lengthens | Risk accumulation function | | | | A firm that fails sooner must score riskier | Focal survival loss | | | | The two objectives' gradients can conflict | Adaptive gradient balancing | | UPSTAR (reconstructed) | Know why each item was bought | Motivation categories are left implicit | Framework of purchase motivations | | | | Inferring motivation usually needs surveys or side data | STB measure from sequences and item attributes only | | | Use motivation to predict the next purchase | The two motivations follow different dynamics | Separate sequence encoders, joined by a learned fusion gate | | | | Exploratory signals are sparse and noisy | Teacher–student distillation from the motivation-specific heads | : The design framework as the spine of a design-science paper. DRDL rows follow the authors' Table 2 [@wang2026drdl]; UPSTAR rows are reconstructed from the published abstract and the released code [@xu2026upstar], not from a table in the paper. {#tbl-sw-design-spine} The table matters because every later section indexes into it. The method section has one subsection per row. The ablation study removes the rows one at a time. The comparison with related methods uses the challenges as its columns. The contribution section restates the goals as design principles. Two failure modes are visible at a glance. A component with no row is decoration, and a referee will ask why it is there. A challenge with no component is a promise the paper never redeems. Each goal usually comes with a kernel theory, a theory from outside the method's field that explains why the design should work. DRDL draws on the chunking theory of memory from cognitive psychology to justify discrete codes. UPSTAR starts from a framework of purchase motivations and keeps the two that are rooted in the consumer's own interests. The kernel theory is inspiration, not a hypothesis under test, and the honest papers say so. DRDL calls it "a principled inspiration". Referees judge it on whether the design traces back to it, not on whether the experiments confirm it. ### The front half: question, gap table, rationale The research questions are design questions, phrased as *how to*. DRDL's two are how to separate useful from redundant information across data views, and how to predict risk over time while respecting two monotonicity constraints. The advice of @sec-sw-open-question still applies, but differently: here the gap is a capability gap, so it has to be shown, not asserted. DRDL shows it with a positioning table of prior studies, with design properties as checkmark columns and "This study" as the last row. The table note states the search rule: studies from 2020–2025 in the AIS Senior Scholars' list of premier journals and in the Academic Journal Guide's operations research and management science category (rated 3 and above), 57 candidates in all. That note turns a literature review into an auditable claim. The table's columns reuse the vocabulary of the design framework. So does a second table, which compares the proposed method with the incumbent methods on the same property columns. Between the literature and the method sits a section that hypothesis-testing papers lack: methodological challenges and design rationale. It argues from the problem's characteristics to each challenge, so that by the time the method appears, every component already has a reason to exist. ### The method section The method section follows a fixed order: a formal problem definition, an overview figure, one subsection per component, and a subsection explaining why the design should work (DRDL §4.7, "Mechanism of Disentanglement"). DRDL is also honest about novelty, a habit worth copying. Its contribution paragraph separates the existing building blocks it reuses, such as vector quantization and the multilayer perceptron, from the five it designed. A referee who finds an uncredited standard component discounts every other novelty claim in the paper. ### Evaluation at three levels Both papers evaluate at three levels, and DRDL names them: model, application, and mechanism. **Model: does it predict better?** DRDL compares against 21 benchmarks from three method families. Sixteen of them are four multitask architectures, each combined with the monotonicity and ranking losses that earlier work proposed for the same two properties. The baselines thus get the best existing fix for each challenge rather than appearing as straw men. It runs five repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation for 50 estimates per cell, plus an out-of-time split. It reports ranking, horizon-specific, and calibration metrics. Two appendices pre-empt the predictable objections. Gradient boosting and parametric survival models on hand-built ratios answer "is the complexity worth it?" Averaging and stacking ensembles answer "isn't this just an ensemble?" The headline is a C-index of 0.775 against 0.712 for the best benchmark on yearly Chinese-market prediction. UPSTAR's abstract reports gains over state-of-the-art recommenders on three retail datasets. **Application: is the gain worth anything?** Offline accuracy is not a decision, so the paper translates it into the currency of the person who acts on it (the same rule as item 8 above). DRDL simulates investment pools and counts the distressed firms each method lets in, scores profitability by return on assets and equity, and repeats the exercise under mean–variance weighting. For a recommender, the equivalent is what the recommendations do for the retailer. UPSTAR's abstract stresses surfacing genuinely exploratory items, which drive discovery and cross-category sales. **Mechanism: why does it work?** "Mechanism" here means something different from Stage 2 of @sec-sw-emb, and it stands on firmer ground. The author controls the artifact, so removing a component is an intervention on the design rather than an inference from observational data. Five kinds of evidence recur: 1. *Ablation tied to the spine.* Drop each component in turn. DRDL removes six, one at a time, and reports the performance gained per unit of training time for each. The mask-based fusion decoder delivers the most gain per second in both markets. 2. *Verify the property each component claims.* If a component claims to disentangle, measure disentanglement directly. DRDL scores its representations on two disentanglement metrics against two disentangled-VAE baselines. A component whose claimed property is never measured has only an ablation to its name, and an ablation cannot say *why* the drop happened. 3. *Locate the gain where the theory predicts it.* UPSTAR's headline mechanism evidence is that the improvement concentrates on exploration-driven purchases. That is where a motivation-aware design should help and a motivation-blind one should struggle. 4. *Rule out the cheap explanations:* more parameters, ensembling, class imbalance. 5. *Sensitivity and interpretability:* vary the hyperparameters the design introduced (codebook size in DRDL, the stable and exploratory cutoffs in UPSTAR), and show what the learned representations encode. DRDL runs seven such analyses, most of them in online appendices. The main text carries the ablation and the property check, because those two tie the evidence back to the spine. ### Make the elaborate version beat the simple one UPSTAR's released code shows why the simple version of your own idea should appear in the paper. In the code, the paper's STB measure works like this. It builds an item co-purchase graph and perturbs it adversarially. It then scores each item by how little its learned embedding moves: robust items count as stable preference, fragile ones as exploratory. Within each customer's history, the top half of items by score are labelled stable and the bottom 40% exploratory. The repository's configuration offers three STB variants. Its help text describes a repurchase-intensity score as "default & best" and the original adversarial version as "degenerate". The repository ships training code but no evaluation script. None of this shows that the published results are wrong, and we have not rerun them. It does show the question a replicator will ask first: does the sophisticated component earn its place over a one-line heuristic for the same construct? The defense is to put that heuristic in the paper as a baseline and beat it. The second defense is to release the code that regenerates the headline table, not only the training loop. ### Carrying the template into a marketing journal Design-science outlets judge the artifact. Marketing journals reading the same paper weigh three further things. - **Validity of any new measure.** A score like STB is a measurement claim: that a number computed from transaction logs tracks a psychological motivation. The standards of @sec-reliability-validity apply. That means convergent evidence against an external criterion, such as stated motivation or a known exploration episode, and discriminant evidence against confounds such as purchase frequency. - **Decision value shown in the field.** An offline accuracy table persuades an IS referee more than a marketing one. A field experiment, or a credible policy counterfactual, carries the application level further. - **The marketing question in front.** UPSTAR's motivation framework is the marketing hook. The architecture is the means. A marketing version of the paper leads with what the framework says about consumers and treats the recommender as the test of that framework. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the design-science method paper 1. Phrase each research question as *how to design* something that achieves a stated property. 2. Build the design framework (@tbl-sw-design-spine) before drafting. Every component gets exactly one challenge, and every challenge gets a component. 3. Name the kernel theory, and present it as inspiration for the design, not a hypothesis the experiments test. 4. Back the gap claim with a positioning table whose selection rule sits in the table note, and reuse its property columns to compare against incumbent methods. 5. Separate reused building blocks from novel ones in the contribution statement. 6. Benchmark across method families, give strong baselines the best existing fix for each challenge, and report variance across repeated splits plus an out-of-time test. 7. Include the simple heuristic version of your own idea, and a tuned off-the-shelf learner on hand-built features, as baselines. 8. Translate accuracy into a decision outcome measured in the user's currency. 9. Ablate one component at a time, measure the property each component claims, and show the gain landing where the kernel theory predicts. 10. State the contribution as design principles, and release code that reproduces the headline table, not only the training loop. ::: ## The Interpretable Machine-Learning Paper: A Competitive-Intelligence Specimen {#sec-sw-interpretable-ml} A second route from machine learning to a top-journal paper is quieter than the design-science route. The paper builds no new architecture. It takes a well-understood probabilistic model, extends it so that it can absorb data the original model never saw, and arranges every estimated parameter so that it answers a question a manager already asks. @qian2026competitive, published in *Production and Operations Management*, is a clean specimen. They extend latent Dirichlet allocation to combine three traces that users leave on a Chinese car platform (the cars they favorite, the cars whose forums they comment in, and what they write there) and return a competitive map of 2,330 car models. @sec-tad-hlda covers the model and reimplements its core on simulated data. This section reads the paper for its construction. (The full open-access article was read; its online appendices were not.) ### The title states the managerial object first The title follows a formula worth copying: *Deriving [a managerial object] from [a data source]: an interpretable machine learning framework*. Competitive intelligence is the object, user behavior data is the input, and the method comes last. An operations or marketing editor sees a question their readers ask before they see an algorithm. Compare a title that leads with the model's name. That title tells the editor what was built but not why anyone should read it. ### Quantify the gap with a number anyone can check Most methods papers assert that prior data are sparse. This one counts. Earlier market-structure work inferred competition from products mentioned together in reviews [@netzer2012]. The authors collected reviews from edmunds.com and autohome.com and found that only 1.1% and 0.13% of them, respectively, mention more than one car. One sentence turns a methodological complaint into a fact a referee can verify, and it motivates the paper's whole design. If co-mentions are that rare, the information has to come from somewhere else, and favorites and comment histories are where it is. ### The spine is a data-source table In @sec-sw-design-science the spine runs from challenges to components. Here it runs from data sources to roles (the paper's Table 1). | Data source | What it reveals | Where it enters the model | |---|---|---| | Favorites lists | Serious consideration, close to purchase | Product embeddings learned from favorites, held fixed | | Commented products | Broader attention, early in search | Topic-model documents; one mixture component draws on the embeddings | | Comment text | Why products are compared | Word topics tied one-to-one to submarkets | : The data-source spine of @qian2026competitive, after their Table 1. {#tbl-sw-hlda-spine} Each row is justified by consumer behavior, not by the method. Favorites and comments are said to capture different stages of the decision process, and the text explains the comparison. The ablation study then removes rows from this table, one source at a time. A reader who sees the table knows what the evaluation will test before reaching it. ### Bound the novelty by naming the building blocks The method section credits its parts. The base models are LDA [@blei2002lda] and Correspondence LDA [@blei2003annotated], the two-component mixture comes from @nguyen2015latentfeature, and the softmax over embeddings follows @dieng2020etm. The new part is the composition: a mixture that lets favorites inform submarkets, a link that makes the text conditional on them, and a joint sampler for both. That claim is smaller than "a new model", and it is one a referee cannot take apart by finding the pieces elsewhere. ### "Interpretable" means every estimand has a managerial name The word *interpretable* in the title is a commitment. It does not mean that a black box gets a post hoc explanation. The paper's section on competitive intelligence (their §3.5) lists four quantities, each a posterior summary of a model parameter and each named for a decision: 1. *Competitive strength* of a product in a submarket: the probability the submarket generates it, mixing comment co-occurrence and the favorites embedding. 2. *User perceptions* of a submarket: the word distribution of its linked topic, scored for sentiment. 3. *User preference* over submarkets: each user's mixture weights. 4. *Submarket popularity*: those weights averaged over users. This mapping is the reason the paper can take an unsupervised model to an operations journal. The reader never has to be told what a topic "means"; the model was built so that each topic is a submarket and each topic weight is a share of attention. ### One focal firm carries the results All the managerial results are told through one company, Tesla. The empirical section finds Tesla's premium EV submarket and its neighbors, ranks the rivals in each, reads the perception topics for each, and predicts where two new entrants will land (an NIO sedan ranks seventh in Tesla's submarket, a BMW only seventeenth). A single running case makes 60 submarkets readable and gives the managerial-implications section something concrete to stand on. ### A validation stack, not a fit statistic The paper presents four layers of evidence. Only the first is in the main text. 1. *Ablation by data source*: five variants, ten runs each, paired *t*-tests against the full model on topic coherence and perplexity. 2. *Parameter recovery*: simulate from the model with known parameters and check that the sampler recovers them. 3. *Benchmarks* against other topic and embedding models. 4. *External validation* against consumer reports, sales data, and human ratings of the submarkets. The fourth layer is what turns a better-fitting model into a claim about markets. Coherence and perplexity are both computed from the model's own outputs. A student copying the template should treat external validation as required, not optional. ### Where the specimen is thin A referee from a marketing journal would press on four points. - **The gains are measured in fit, and they are small.** Against single-source variants, the full model improves coherence by about 5% and perplexity by about 4%. The variants that pair favorites with comments come within 3% on coherence. One ordering in the ablation also goes the other way. Adding text to comments without favorites makes both metrics *worse* than comments alone, so text helps only when the favorites embedding anchors the submarkets. The paper reads the ablation as showing that favorites are the most valuable source. It does not discuss why adding text alone lowers fit. - **Strength is attention, not substitution.** A product's competitive strength is the share of a submarket's comment and favorites activity it attracts. The demand definition of a market is about who substitutes for whom [@desarbo2006competes; @ringel2016asymmetric]. Agreement with sales patterns, in an appendix, is consistent with substitution but does not establish it. - **The number of submarkets was chosen by perplexity**, which tends to keep improving as topics are added, and the 60 submarkets are then read by hand. - **The new-entrant forecast relies on vector arithmetic chosen by the analyst.** It approximates the Mercedes EQC as Audi e-tron − Audi Q7 + Mercedes GLC. The analogy is checked visually for one car. It is not tested on a set of launches whose later positions are known. None of these is fatal. Each is a place where a revision would ask for one more table. No code or data were released, which leaves the gains impossible to check from outside. ### Carrying the template into a marketing journal The acknowledgments show that the paper was handled in *POM* by marketing scholars, so the genre already sits on the marketing–operations border. A version aimed at a marketing journal would keep the spine and the named estimands and add three things. It would validate submarkets against substitution measured from choice or consideration data. It would add a held-out prediction test, for example the following year's cross-shopping or the positions of cars launched after the training window. And it would make one managerial decision visibly depend on the map. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the interpretable machine-learning paper 1. Put the managerial object first in the title and the method last. 2. Quantify the data gap that motivates the method with a count a referee can reproduce. 3. Build the data-source table before drafting: each source gets a behavioral rationale and a place in the model. 4. Extend a model readers already trust, and name every borrowed building block. 5. Map every estimated parameter to a quantity with a managerial name, and define the mapping by equation. 6. Tell the results through one focal firm. 7. Ablate by data source with repeated runs and paired tests, and explain any ordering that contradicts the story. 8. Add parameter recovery on simulated data and external validation against outcomes the model never saw. 9. Include a prediction the incumbent methods cannot make, and test it on held-out cases rather than one illustration. 10. Release code and, where licensing allows, the processed data. ::: ## The Structural-Model Paper: A Consumer-Search Specimen {#sec-sw-structural} A third paper from the same September 2026 issue of *Information Systems Research* shows a different genre, the empirical structural-model paper. @zhang2026footprints model how consumers search across a platform's native app and its mini-program, carrying a reference price from one channel to the other, and use the estimates to design a promotion (@sec-click-search-mss covers the substance). The artifact here is not a method to be benchmarked, as in @sec-sw-design-science, nor a causal effect, as in @sec-sw-emb. It is an *estimated model of behavior*, and the contribution is what the model lets a decision maker do that a reduced-form analysis cannot. Structural papers in marketing, economics, and IS share a skeleton, and this one shows it clearly. (Only the two versions of the abstract and the deposited reference list were accessible when this section was written, so what follows reads the paper's framing, not its internals.) ### The title and the abstract The title has two halves joined by a colon, a phenomenon and a model: "Analyzing Consumer Footprints on E-Commerce Platforms: A Multichannel Sequential Search Model with Reference Price." The first half echoes @ghose2019modeling, "Modeling Consumer Footprints on Search Engines," and that echo positions the paper in an IS tradition before the reader reaches the abstract. The second half lists the model's ingredients in order of novelty: *multichannel* is new, *sequential search* is the inherited framework, and *reference price* is the behavioral addition. The Crossref abstract makes six moves in seven sentences, and each is one or two sentences long: 1. **Context.** Mini-programs let consumers browse across the app and the mini-program, leaving click and purchase records in both. 2. **Opportunity.** These multichannel footprints contain information about search preferences that could improve multichannel management. 3. **Gap.** Prior studies focus on single-channel contexts that "may not directly apply." 4. **Model.** A threefold search across channels, products, and pages, with a reference price updated along the journey. 5. **Findings.** Heterogeneity in channel preferences, cross-channel costs, and reference-price sensitivity explains the variety of footprints. 6. **Policy.** A 32% average promotion gap between channels, and more profit from a smaller promotion than the state-of-the-art model achieves. A second abstract, on the paper's record in City University of Hong Kong's repository and marked "© 2026, INFORMS", swaps move 5 for a prediction claim ("significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art sequential search models in predicting both clicks and purchases") and quantifies move 6 as a 22% profit improvement. That pairing is the genre's signature: the model is first shown to be *right* (it predicts held-out behavior better than the incumbent model) and then shown to be *useful* (it changes a decision, by an amount in money). ### The spine: data feature, model component, counterfactual lever The design-science paper is held together by a table of challenges and components (@tbl-sw-design-spine). The structural paper's equivalent links three things: a *feature of the data* that the incumbent model cannot reproduce, the *model component* added to reproduce it, and the *counterfactual lever* that the component makes available. A component that changes no counterfactual is hard to justify; a lever with no component behind it is a promise the paper cannot keep. | Paper | Data feature | Model component | Counterfactual lever | |---|---|---|---| | Zhang et al. (2026) | Same products, two channels, different prices | Cross-channel search with channel-specific costs | Channel-specific promotion | | | Prices seen early shape later clicks | Reference price updated along the journey | Promotion *gap* between channels | | | Results arrive in pages | Cross-page search cost | (inherited from ranking work) | | | Channels are linked by external links | Channel entry and switching costs | Aligning links with promotions | | Hu & Karacaoglu (2024) | Mini-program sessions are longer and convert more | Fixed (entry) and marginal (per-click) search costs by channel | Referral credits on WeChat; coupons on the app | : The structural paper's spine. Zhang et al. rows are reconstructed from the published abstracts; Hu & Karacaoglu rows follow their accepted manuscript [@hu2024westore]. {#tbl-sw-structural-spine} The table also says where to spend pages. The paper has to show *model-free evidence* for every data feature in the first column before the model appears (for example, that consumers who saw a lower price in one channel click differently in the other), because a referee who does not believe the feature will not believe the component. ### The sections, and what each must contain A structural search paper usually runs in this order. 1. **Introduction**, ending with the policy number and a contribution paragraph for each literature the paper joins. This paper joins three, as its reference list shows: consumer search (Weitzman-type models from @weitzman1979optimal to @morozov2021estimation), reference prices (@mazumdar2005reference; @putler1992incorporating), and multichannel and mobile commerce. The contribution claim works because the three have rarely been combined. That is the "intersection" gap of @sec-sw-contribution, and it holds only if the intersection is really empty, which leads to the next item. 2. **Literature**, organized by stream, closing each stream with what this paper adds. The closest prior work deserves a paragraph of its own. The nearest predecessor here is @hu2024westore, a *Production and Operations Management* paper on the same app versus mini-program comparison, estimated on JD.com data with a sequential search model. It does not appear in the ISR paper's deposited reference list. Whether the two were developed in parallel we cannot tell. The lesson for authors is general: search the adjacent fields (operations, IS, economics) for the closest competitor, because a referee from that field will know it. 3. **Data and model-free evidence.** Sessions, channels, click order, prices, and purchases, with descriptive patterns tied to the spine's first column. 4. **Model.** Utility, search costs, the reference-price process, and the decision rules, stated as equations, with every departure from the canonical model flagged. A reference price that updates with prices seen during the search breaks one of Weitzman's independence assumptions. An honest paper says what the consumer is assumed to anticipate and what she is not. 5. **Identification.** Which variation in the data pins down which parameter: click order for preferences, stopping for search costs, cross-channel price differences for the reference-price parameters. The framework of @ursu2025sequential is now the standard reference for this argument. 6. **Estimation**: the simulator, its tuning, and a Monte Carlo study showing that the estimator recovers known parameters (@sec-click-search-sim does this for a stylized version). 7. **Results**: parameter estimates, heterogeneity, and fit against benchmark search models and machine-learning predictors (this paper's reference list includes a deep click-prediction model, xDeepFM). 8. **Counterfactuals.** The policy simulation, compared against the policy the benchmark model would have recommended. Choose counterfactuals the normalizations permit: price and promotion changes rather than search-cost changes. 9. **Robustness and conclusion.** ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the structural search paper 1. Make the title name the phenomenon first and the model second. 2. Build the spine (@tbl-sw-structural-spine) before drafting: every new component answers a data feature and opens a counterfactual lever. 3. Show model-free evidence for each data feature before the model. 4. Flag every departure from the canonical model, and say what it costs in optimality or identification. 5. Argue identification parameter by parameter, from the variation in the data. 6. Run a Monte Carlo recovery study for the estimator and report the tuning choices. 7. Beat the incumbent structural model *and* a flexible predictive model out of sample. 8. Run counterfactuals the normalizations allow, and compare against the incumbent model's recommendation. 9. Search adjacent fields for the closest prior paper and position against it explicitly. ::: ## The Observational Contagion Paper: A Fraud-Spread Specimen {#sec-sw-contagion-template} Many marketing and finance questions are about spread: of word of mouth, of a product, of a misconduct norm, of an investing habit. Usually there is no experiment and no clean shock, only outcomes by place or person and a measured network. Papers in this genre cannot claim identification in the strict sense, so their persuasiveness depends on structure. @griffin2026fraud, on fraud in the U.S. Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), is a well-built recent example from *The Review of Financial Studies*. The econometrics, with our replication from the authors' package, are in @sec-graph-exposure. This section reads the paper as a piece of writing. ### Title and abstract The title is a yes-or-no question with a subtitle naming the setting: "Is Fraud Contagious? Social Connections and the Looting of COVID Relief Programs." The question repeats the title of @dimmock2018fraud, who asked it about coworkers at financial-advisory firms. Reusing a known question tells finance readers which literature the paper extends before they read a word of the abstract. The subtitle supplies the channel (social connections) and a vivid object ("looting"). The abstract makes four moves in four sentences. It states a fact: fraud is geographically concentrated. It states the main finding: high-fraud places are socially linked, and fraud spreads over time along those links. It gives mechanism evidence: members of fraud-promoting social media groups commit more fraud, and linked places use the same FinTech lenders. It closes with policy: faster, data-driven detection and prosecution. The abstract has no identification jargon. The identification argument starts in the introduction. ### Rival hypotheses before the favored one Section 1.2 sets out three hypotheses before any result. The first is an individualist null: some people were more willing to commit fraud and took the chance. If so, local crime, culture and demographics should explain where fraud happened, and social ties should add nothing. The second is organized cybercrime using stolen identities, which predicts a link to past identity theft. The third, social transmission, is grounded in Sutherland's differential-association theory of crime: people learn both the techniques and the rationalizations for an offense from their contacts. The paper then gives the first two hypotheses a real test. Section 2 regresses fraud on demographics, religious affiliation, public corruption, identity theft, suspicious-activity reports and social capital, and it reports what works (identity theft, poverty, race) as partial support for both. Only then does the social measure arrive, and it wins on incremental $R^2$: it explains about ten times as much within-county variation as the strongest demographic variable. Giving the favored hypothesis a fair fight against named rivals is more persuasive than testing it alone. It also answers in advance the referee who asks "isn't this just poverty?" ### The spine: one section per referee question After the main estimate, every subsection heading in Section 3 is a question a skeptical reader would ask, and each is answered by one exhibit. | Section | Heading, as the reader's question | Worry it answers | Main exhibit | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | 2 | Is fraud explained by demographics, corruption, crime? | Individual propensity | County and ZIP regressions | | 3.1 | (Social proximity to suspicious lending) | Is the effect large? | Coefficients plus incremental $R^2$ | | 3.2 | Concentrated in particular areas? | One subgroup drives it | Coefficient plot by median split | | 3.3 | Do connections explain the spread over time? | Static correlation | Decile heat map; matched pairs; lagged regression | | 3.4 | Driven by nearby regions? | Physical spillover | Binscatter; distance-restricted regressions | | 3.5 | Homophily or omitted variables? | Reflection problem | Five numbered responses, ending in an Oster bound | | 4 | Mechanisms | What actually travelled? | Social media groups; identical-loan clusters; lender choice | : How @griffin2026fraud arranges its evidence. Headings paraphrased from the published paper. {#tbl-sw-contagion-spine} Building this table before drafting is the most useful thing to take from the specimen. List the worries a referee will raise, give each one a heading and an exhibit, and order them from the most obvious alternative to the most subtle. Section 3.5 is the section referees read most closely. The paper names the threat by its canonical source, Manski's reflection problem [@manski1993reflection]. It concedes that the threat is hard to eliminate. It then lists five numbered responses, each pointing back to evidence already shown. Conceding the limit first makes the numbered responses easier to trust. ### Moves worth copying - **Description first.** Figure 1 shows a county map, then within-county variation across ZIP codes, then fraud rates over time by lender type. The reader sees the variation to be explained before any model tries to explain it. - **A network figure that makes an argument.** Figure 2 places ZIP codes of three cities on the sides of a triangle, sorted by fraud decile, with edge width showing tie strength. High-fraud nodes visibly connect to each other. Most network plots show only that a network exists. This one shows the result. - **Magnitude in a portable unit.** All variables are standardized, so every coefficient reads in standard deviations, and the incremental-$R^2$ comparison gives a sentence readers remember ("ten times the next predictor"). - **Fingerprint outcomes as mechanism evidence.** The strongest section concerns outcomes that homophily cannot easily produce: clusters of loans identical in industry, amount and headcount, and the choice of a particular FinTech platform. A refrain recurs at the end of each mechanism test, that the pattern would be "difficult to explain if social connections merely proxy for homophily." Repeating one sentence ties the separate tests to a single claim. - **Qualitative texture.** Group names and posts from fraud-promoting social media groups ("sauce", "methods"), and word clouds contrasting high- and low-fraud groups, make the mechanism concrete. The full posts go in an appendix exhibit. Differential-association theory explains why both techniques and rationalizations show up in them. - **Robustness in footnotes.** The body states each robustness result in one sentence and points to the Internet Appendix, which has about twenty tables. Weighting and clustering are stated once in a footnote and then kept the same throughout. - **Calibrated language.** The heterogeneity results "may alleviate (though not eliminate)" concerns about omitted variables. Hedges like that one show readers the authors know where the evidence stops. - **Policy that follows from the finding.** The policy point concerns speed: fraud spreading through networks outran the program's pay-now, chase-later model. That conclusion depends on the spread result, so it does not read as an afterthought. ### Where the specimen is thin A referee reading the paper with @sec-graph-exposure open would press on three points. First, linked places can be *targeted* together, for example by social media advertising. That is a common shock that travels along ties, and none of the tests separates it from person-to-person transmission. Second, the network is measured in 2021, after the program began, so the design assumes ties predate the fraud. Third, the Oster bound depends on the assumed maximum $R^2$ (@sec-causal-oster), and the paper uses one value. None of these sinks the paper, but a manuscript of this genre should raise each point itself, in Section 3.5's list, before the referee does. ### Carrying the template into a marketing journal The same skeleton fits a word-of-mouth or adoption paper using place-level outcomes and the public county-to-county Social Connectedness Index [@bailey2018connectedness]. The contribution paragraph should name which of four evidence types the paper supplies, because marketing referees will rank them. A shock to the network itself, as in @dimmock2018fraud's use of firm mergers, ranks highest. Next comes a shock to one's contacts that does not touch oneself, as in @bailey2018housing. A fingerprint outcome ranks third, as in @maturana2019teachers's same-lender choices among teachers. A stacked falsification battery alone comes last. The specimen combines the third and fourth. Say plainly which ones you have, and title the effect accordingly: "social transmission is consistent with" is a defensible claim from a battery, "the causal peer effect is" is not. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the observational contagion paper 1. Ask the question in the title; if a well-known paper asked it in another setting, echo that title. 2. State rival hypotheses before the favored one, with the prediction each makes, and give the rivals a real test. 3. Show the raw variation (maps, within-unit spread, time paths) before any regression. 4. Define the exposure measure as an equation, and exclude the nearest units (own county, own firm) so it cannot be mechanical. 5. Report magnitude in a portable unit: standardized coefficients plus incremental $R^2$. 6. Build the spine (@tbl-sw-contagion-spine): one heading per referee worry, one exhibit per heading. 7. Name the reflection problem explicitly, concede what cannot be ruled out, then list your responses. 8. Find at least one fingerprint outcome that only shared information could produce. 9. Add qualitative evidence of what was transmitted, with the raw material in an appendix. 10. State weighting, clustering and standardization once, and keep them fixed across tables. Standardized coefficients change with the standardization sample. 11. Rank your evidence type against shock-based designs and phrase the causal claim to match. ::: ## The Theory-Building Paper: Naming a Construct from Hidden Data {#sec-sw-theory-building} Some papers earn their place by changing how a field looks at a phenomenon. They name a construct nobody had named, show how to observe it, sort its variants, and end with what institutions should do about it. This is the inductive theory-building paper. It is the house genre of *Organization Science*, *Administrative Science Quarterly*, and the *Academy of Management Journal*, and marketing journals publish it too, in consumer culture theory and in conceptual-empirical work. It is hard to learn from the hypothesis-testing template, because the contribution is not an estimate. It is a concept, a classification of the concept's forms, and an argument about where a boundary lies. @weiss2026criminal is a clean specimen. The authors ask how entrepreneurs carry out criminal deception, meaning the use of deceptive means to defraud audiences. They answer from the court records of 12 Silicon Valley technology ventures whose founders were prosecuted for securities, wire, or bank fraud between 2000 and 2023. The answer is a new construct, *façading*. Entrepreneurs construct, perform, and protect an illusory appearance of a high-growth venture that masks the venture's actual underperformance, and they do it in three forms keyed to how far the venture has fallen behind what its audiences expect. The paper closes with remedies addressed to the SEC, to investors, and to entrepreneurship educators. (This section was written from the authors' accepted manuscript [@weiss2026criminalpreprint]. Section and table numbers follow that version and may differ slightly in print.) ### The spine: one construct, three sub-processes, three forms The paper makes ten moves, and each one transfers to other topics. | Move | Where it sits | What @weiss2026criminal do | What to copy | |---|---|---|---| | Name an unstudied trajectory | Introduction | Prior work treats deception as dramatized storytelling. The unstudied path is the slide from dramatization into criminal deception | Place the phenomenon on a continuum the field already accepts, and point to the segment nobody has studied | | Anchor in public cases | Introduction | Nikola's demo truck rolled down a slope; Frank fabricated a customer dataset ten times its real size | Open with one or two named public examples before the anonymized data | | Choose a lens that spans two literatures | Introduction; Theoretical Motivation | The discourse–organizing interface. Cultural entrepreneurship studies the stories, wrongdoing research studies causes and effects, and neither studies the organizing that makes a lie hold up | Show that each literature owns half the phenomenon. Borrow the distinction from precedent (their footnote 1) instead of coining one | | Get past the observability barrier | Methods: Dataset | Federal court records from PACER, filtered by statute, district, venture age, and funding type | Find the archive in which the hidden behavior was forced into the open, and write the sample as a filter someone could rerun | | Define the construct from an existing one | Introduction; Data Analysis | *Façade*, an established organizational concept, becomes *façading*, a process with three sub-processes | Start from a definition readers accept, extend it, and give the extension parts a coder can find | | Operationalize the parts | Data Analysis, Steps 2–4 | Facets deceived (narrow: one or two; expansive: more), audience (novice or expert), protection approach | Turn every part of the definition into a coding rule | | Explain the variation | Data Analysis, Step 5; Table 3 | The form of façading tracks the size of the expectation–reality gap, which tracks the venture's life-cycle stage | Name the one dimension that sorts the cases, and report the rival explanations checked first | | Report findings as a grid | Findings | Three forms × three sub-processes, in the same order in every subsection | Give every cell of the typology the same internal structure | | Draw the theory | Figure 1 | Expected and actual performance over the life cycle, with the gap shaded | Make the construct a visible quantity in one picture | | Turn mechanism into remedy | Practical Implications | Whistleblower protection for startup employees, SEC audits of late-stage ventures, investor accountability, education | Derive each remedy from a finding, and address it to a named institution | : The architecture of an inductive theory-building paper, read from @weiss2026criminal. {#tbl-sw-theory-spine} ### Seeing something new The paper's new way of looking rests on three reframings, and none of them needs new vocabulary. 1. *From discourse to the discourse–organizing interface.* Earlier work studied the stories entrepreneurs tell. This paper studies the organizing that lets a false story survive checking: the doctored invoices, forged term sheets, staged demos, and impersonated reference calls. 2. *From the future to the past.* The earlier literature treats deception as part of future-making, in the form of aspirational claims about what a venture will do. The prosecuted founders fabricated what the venture had already done: booked revenue, recurring customers, a completed audit. The authors argue that fictionalizing the past is the hallmark of the criminal form. 3. *From the entrepreneur to the institution.* Silicon Valley's unicorn ideal sets what audiences expect at each stage, so the gap founders backfill is set by the ecosystem, not only by their own pitches. Each reframing is a contrast a referee can check against the literature cited, and that is what makes it defensible. A lens the referee cannot check against prior work reads as a label. Positioning against the nearest neighbor takes one clause. The paper cites a 2022 working paper by Mohliver, Karp, and Zuzul titled *Dominant Deceptions*, which appears to be an earlier version of @zuzul2026dominant. That project follows a single venture and traces how deception spreads inside it. @weiss2026criminal describe that work as being about how deception diffuses within ventures, and they claim a different question: how deception is carried out, compared across ventures. Both papers build on an expectation–reality gap, and their answers fit together. One traces the drift from "we will" to "we have" inside one firm. The other sorts the finished schemes across firms. When a close competitor exists, name it, say which question it answers, and claim a different one. ### Defining the construct The definition is built in three steps. It starts from a noun the field already uses. In the organizational definition the authors adopt, a façade is a symbolic front that reassures stakeholders of the organization's legitimacy. The noun then becomes a process, façading. Finally, the process is split into sub-processes a coder can find in a document: - *constructing* the façade, through fictionalized stories, fabricated evidence, staged product demos, co-opted verification, and manipulated regulatory compliance; - *performing* it before the audiences that hold resources; - *protecting* it from scrutiny. A construct also needs a boundary, because a construct defined only by its center gets stretched to fit everything (@sec-construct-vs-variable). The paper draws the line between ordinary entrepreneurial dramatization and criminal deception. Entrepreneurs cross it when their stories become detached from the venture's operational reality and are propped up by organized fabrication of evidence. That boundary is what makes the construct useful, because it tells an educator, an investor, or a juror which side of the line a given act falls on. The typology is cumulative. Surface façading fictionalizes stories of imminent success. Reinforced façading adds interlocking sets of faked historical evidence and central control of information. Deep façading adds faked product demos, co-opted due diligence, manipulated regulatory compliance, and organized secrecy. Each form contains the acts of the one before it (their Table 3). That makes the scheme easy to apply and hard to dispute at the margins. The authors also report what they did not see. They call the process discontinuous because no venture in the data moved from one form to the next, and they say such a progression is possible but unobserved. ### Measuring it: data that make the hidden visible Criminal deception is hidden by design, which is why earlier research theorized it mostly through its causes and consequences. The paper's main methodological move is to find data in which the hidden part is already documented. Court records are produced adversarially. Prosecutors must prove each deceptive act with exhibits, and defendants contest the evidence. The sample is defined as a filter a reader could rerun: - federal securities-fraud charges and the related wire, bank, and conspiracy statutes; - the Northern District of California; - cases between 2000 and 2023; - privately held, equity-financed, high-growth technology ventures; - fraud within ten years of founding. The filter excludes public companies, fraud tied to an IPO, and SEC investigations that settled or closed without a public record. A second search then collects every further case against the same founders. The analysis section is unusually long, and the authors say why: inductive analysis of court records is rare in organization science. It has five steps: 1. selecting documents (complaints, indictments, plea agreements, sentencing memoranda, and trial transcripts, but not procedural filings); 2. in vivo coding of the first three ventures; 3. building a codebook by moving between the data and the literature; 4. drawing a timeline for each venture, with its funding rounds overlaid; 5. comparing the twelve cases. Two choices are worth copying. In the last step, the authors built tables to test rival explanations before settling on the life-cycle gap. They checked whether sophistication depended on how early the deception began, and on how long it lasted. They also pseudonymized every venture although the records are public, because the aim is patterns across cases, not singling out deviant individuals. The headline numbers in the introduction can be checked against the paper's own Table 1. Run this check on your own manuscript before you submit it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # The 12 ventures of Weiss & Radoynovska (2026), from their Tables 1 and 3. # capital_musd: equity capital raised, $ million. prison_months: summed over all # defendants (founders, co-founders, executives); The most sophisticated form is therefore observed through the deepest records, and records are deepest where a defendant fought the charges. A referee could fairly ask whether part of what separates the forms is documentation rather than behavior, since a guilty plea leaves a thin file. The rival explanations the authors report concern timing and duration, not record depth. If your data source's coverage varies with your construct, say so, and show that the construct holds among cases with comparable records. The gap itself can be measured with numbers, which points to a quantitative follow-up. Evidence that would only repeat what the previous form already showed goes to an online appendix (footnotes 6 and 9 say so), and the main text shows only what is new at each level. A reader can turn to any cell of the three-by-three grid and find the same structure. ### Drawing the theory The paper's Figure 1 puts the theory in one picture. It states four numbered arguments before it mentions any literature: 1. Façading backfills the gap between expected and actual performance. 2. The form of façading depends on the size of the gap. 3. The theory sits at the discourse–organizing interface. 4. The venture's projected appearance becomes progressively detached from its reality. The fourth argument climbs a ladder of metaphors: a veneer laid over the real venture, then a standalone artifact that audiences deal with instead of the venture, then a staged parallel world like the one in *The Truman Show*. Each metaphor names a different level of detachment, so the ladder adds content rather than decoration. Only then come the contributions, one subsection for each of three literatures (cultural entrepreneurship, organizational wrongdoing, and the social effects of entrepreneurship), and each ends with a research agenda. One claim is built to be quoted and argued with: verifiability, not authenticity, is the right guard against deception, because authenticity judgments reward the rule-breaking and hubris that entrepreneurial culture already prizes. A contrarian claim that can be tested is often the sentence later papers cite. ### Proposing a solution The practical implications say who should act and how. Lower the barriers to whistleblowing, and extend SEC whistleblower protection to startup employees. Introduce SEC audits of ventures late in the life cycle. Hold investors who sit on boards more accountable, and have them check claims against several independent sources during due diligence. Teach entrepreneurship students where permissible dramatization ends and criminal façading begins. The remedies also enter a live debate in legal scholarship over whether the SEC should police private markets, which gives the paper readers beyond its own field. FTC complaints and consent orders, National Advertising Division decisions, state attorney-general actions, and class-action filings all document deceptive claims with exhibits, as these court records do. The construct travels too. One deep-façading venture sold "AI" insights that were partly produced by paid human workers watching videos, the pattern now called AI washing. Greenwashing, fake reviews, and vaporware announcements (@sec-market-entry) are other cases in which a claim and the organizing behind it can come apart. Three adjustments help a marketing version get through review. - **Put the market stake in front.** A marketing referee will ask what the construct changes for buyers, competitors, or regulators, not only for theory. - **Pair the typology with a measure that scales.** The coding rules in @tbl-sw-theory-spine (facets deceived, audience, protection approach) can become labels for a text classifier run over thousands of enforcement documents (@sec-text-as-data). A claimed-to-actual ratio like the one above is a continuous measure of the gap. The typology then becomes a hypothesis the next study can test at scale. - **State the boundary as a decision rule.** The line between dramatization and criminal deception has a counterpart in advertising law, the line between puffery and a material misrepresentation. A paper that tells readers which side of it a claim falls on is useful to managers and regulators alike. ### A second specimen: a construct that sits between two literatures @giuliani2026doublefailure build the same kind of paper from a different kind of hidden data. Their question is why workers stay at a plant they know is harming them and their families. The site is the ILVA steel plant in Taranto, Italy, which by 2013 employed about 12,000 workers, relied on 8,000 contractors, and produced about a quarter of Italy's steel. Each relevant literature covers half of the case (checklist item 3 below). Organizational research treats employees as *insiders* who rationalize or go along with wrongdoing. Research on victims and environmental justice treats communities as *victims* seeking redress from institutions. These workers are both. The data design deals with the main threat to an interview study of a past scandal, which is that people reinterpret it in hindsight. The authors fixed two critical incidents. The first was the 2008 dioxin crisis, which ended with about 1,200 contaminated sheep slaughtered. The second was a 2012 court order seizing the plant's hot furnaces. They then built a database of workers' quotations recorded at the time: over 3,000 pages of newspapers and books and about 17 hours of television, with each quotation coded to its incident. Only after that did they add 56 interviews conducted between 2020 and 2025 (about 63 hours). The 232 coded quotations show how workers' framing changed between the two incidents, not just how they remember it. The construct is defined by what it is not, and that is the move to copy. *Organizational resignation* means staying while condemning the firm, as a way to survive. The authors separate it in turn from loyalty, which defends the firm; from complicity and rationalization, which excuse the wrongdoing; from apathy, which drops the grievance; and from the victimhood of residents, who do not work there. *Institutional abandonment* is the belief that no outside authority will protect the workers. It builds up through repeated encounters with courts, regulators, and politicians that deny or delay recognition. The *double-failure trap* is the two beliefs reinforcing each other. The authors draw its boundary by comparison with single-failure cases, in which one arena, such as a court or a firm committed to repair, still offers a way out. A marketing version of the question is easy to state, although the paper does not pose it: a customer, supplier, or employee who keeps dealing with a brand they condemn is resigned, not loyal, and a satisfaction survey that reads continued business as approval will classify them wrongly. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the theory-building paper 1. Build the construct from a definition readers accept, split it into sub-processes a coder can find, and state the boundary where it stops applying. 6. Make every headline number recomputable from a table in the paper. ::: ## The Measurement Paper: A New Variable from Text {#sec-sw-measurement} A measurement paper names something that matters and that no dataset records, builds a variable for it from a source nobody had mined for that purpose, and then spends most of its pages showing that the variable behaves the way the thing itself should. The contribution is the variable. The regressions are there to earn the reader's trust in it, and none of them needs to identify a causal effect. Finance and accounting publish this genre steadily, with text-based measures of competition, financial constraints, corporate culture, and brand value among the well-known cases [@li2021culture; @boustanifar2025brand], and it is the most direct route by which unstructured data (@sec-text-as-data) becomes a top-journal paper. @boustanifar2026intangible is a specimen worth taking apart because the method is as simple as the genre allows. The measure is a word count. Whatever persuades the reader therefore comes from the architecture of the paper, and that architecture can be copied. The authors start from an accounting rule. A liability goes on the balance sheet only if it is probable and can be reliably estimated. Anything else, such as a pending lawsuit, a product-liability exposure, an environmental obligation, or a false-advertising or patent-infringement claim, is disclosed in the text of the annual report and nowhere in the numbers. They call these obligations *intangible liabilities* (IL), count the words that signal them in every 10-K filed between fiscal years 1996 and 2020, and show that the count predicts lawsuits, reputational damage, valuation, stock returns, and crash risk. (This section was written from the authors' accepted manuscript [@boustanifar2023intangiblewp], in its April 2026 revision marked as forthcoming in *Management Science*. A reader who stops after the abstract already knows what the construct is and why it has stakes. That matters more in this genre than in most, because there is no clever identification strategy to carry the reader's interest. ### Defining the construct before measuring it The definition is borrowed from a rule, which makes the boundary of the construct checkable. An intangible liability is an economically significant obligation that fails the recognition test (probable and estimable) and so appears only in text. A footnote then separates it from the neighboring accounting category. Disclosed contingent liabilities are a subset, because a firm can be exposed to a kind of harm, such as personal injury from its products, before any claim exists, and that exposure is written up under risk factors. The footnote is also the argument for measuring over the whole filing. A measure built only on the legal-proceedings section would capture the subset and miss the construct. A second footnote settles what "intangible" means. It is not "cannot be touched." It is "cannot be appraised at an actual or approximate value." Human capital can be touched and is off the balance sheet. A firm's cryptocurrency cannot be touched and is on it. Two sentences of this kind close off the most likely misreading of a new label, and a new construct should always get them (@sec-construct-vs-variable). The positioning against prior work is equally short. Accounting research already measures *litigation risk*, the probability of being sued [@kim2012litigation]. The authors grant that it is one source of intangible liabilities and list others that it leaves out: pending suits, recalls, guarantees, environmental obligations, and pending legislation. They later add litigation-risk measures as controls. The claim is that the new construct is broader than its nearest neighbor, and the paper supports the claim with a definition in the front and a regression in the back. ### Building the measure, and the three decisions inside a word count A dictionary measure looks like it involves no decisions. This one involves three, and the paper defends each. *Which words.* The starting list was built to measure tone, so many of its entries are legalistic words with no bearing on obligations (*hereby*, *shall*, *aforementioned*). The authors read how each word is used in filings before deciding. *Interrogate* appears in biotech filings about interrogating cells. *Designator* is an airline code. *Extracorporeal* is a medical procedure. All three go. The parent list is also unigram-only and correctly omits *liability*, which is neutral in a financial statement. The new list adds bigrams such as *product liability*, *environmental liability*, *false advertising*, and *filed suit*, which carry the meaning that the single word does not. For a marketing reader, the dictionary is in part a list of marketing-made obligations: *false advertising*, *deceptive*, *product liability*, *recall*, *warranty defect*, *counterfeit*, *unfair competition*. *How to weight.* Every term counts equally. The cited justification is a comparison of methods in the disclosure literature, which finds equal-weighted, domain-specific word counts about as powerful as more elaborate schemes, provided the list excludes words that also appear in other contexts [@henry2016tone]. That is why so much of the effort goes into pruning. *How to scale.* The main measure is the log of the raw count, with the log of filing length entered as a control. The authors argue against the usual share-of-words scaling. In sentiment work every word is positive, negative, or neutral, so a share is natural. Here the researcher is looking for one kind of content inside a document that is mostly about other things, and dividing by length lets differences in length drive the variation. Where a control is impossible, as in portfolio sorts, they fall back on the share. The scaling decision has consequences that a short simulation makes visible. In their Table 3 the coefficient of the log count on log filing length is about 1.2, so dictionary hits grow faster than the filing does. The simulation below builds that in. It is our illustration and uses no data from the paper. Each filing has a latent exposure that the researcher never sees, a length, and a count of dictionary hits that depends on both. The outcome depends on exposure and, separately and negatively, on length. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # A stylized illustration written for this section; none of it is the paper's data. set.seed(41) n <- 20000 theta <- rnorm(n) # latent exposure, never observed len <- 10 + 0.74 * rnorm(n) # log words in the filing count <- rpois(n, exp(4.3 + 0.5 * theta + 1.2 * (len - 10))) # dictionary hits y <- 1.0 * theta - 0.5 * (len - 10) + rnorm(n, sd = 3) # long filings do worse z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x)) log_count <- log(1 + count) share <- count / exp(len) resid_ct <- resid(lm(log_count ~ len)) # log count net of filing length slope <- function(f) unname(coef(lm(f))[2]) scaling <- data.frame( measure = c("Log count, no length control", "Share of total words", "Log count, length controlled", "Latent exposure (infeasible)"), cor_with_exposure = c(cor(log_count, theta), cor(share, theta), cor(resid_ct, theta), 1), cor_with_length = c(cor(log_count, len), cor(share, len), cor(resid_ct, len), cor(theta, len)), slope_per_sd = c(slope(y ~ z(log_count)), slope(y ~ z(share)), slope(y ~ z(resid_ct) + len), slope(y ~ z(theta) + len)) ) scaling[-1] <- round(scaling[-1], 2) print(scaling, row.names = FALSE) #> measure cor_with_exposure cor_with_length slope_per_sd #> Log count, no length control 0.48 0.86 0.14 #> Share of total words 0.87 0.26 0.74 #> Log count, length controlled 0.96 0.00 0.92 #> Latent exposure (infeasible) 1.00 0.00 0.96 ``` ::: The raw log count is mostly a measure of how long the filing is, and its slope on the outcome is close to zero because the length effect cancels the exposure effect. The share does much better, but it still loads on length, because hits grow faster than words, and it recovers only about three-quarters of the true slope. The log count with length controlled comes close to the infeasible benchmark. Two things follow for anyone building a count-based measure. Estimate the elasticity of the count to document length before choosing a scaling, since a share is right only when that elasticity is one. And when two versions of the measure appear in one paper, say which result rests on which. ### The validation ladder The paper never claims that its dictionary is accurate. The generic words that dominate the count (@tbl-sw-measurement-package) appear in filings with nothing at stake. The validation is entirely by association with outcomes. A marketing journal would normally ask for agreement with human judgment as well (@sec-classification-validity). - *The simplest rival is beaten off the page.* A footnote reports that the parent dictionary shows no robust relation to future lawsuits, reputation, or returns. This is the comparison that justifies all the pruning, and it is described as unreported. It should be a table (@sec-sw-design-science makes the same point about method papers). - *The legal outcome is narrower than the construct.* The lawsuits are securities class actions, which shareholders bring. The construct's own examples are product, environmental, and intellectual-property claims. The two are related, since a product disaster often triggers a shareholder suit, but the validation outcome is not the obligation the paper defines. - *Filing length does a lot of work.* Adding length and three accounting ratios lifts the explained variance of IL from 0.51 to 0.75. In the return regressions, length carries a coefficient of $-0.17$ beside IL's $+0.16$. The finding is therefore about liability language relative to the length of the filing, and long filings alone predict lower returns. The simulation above shows why this must be stated plainly, and the IBM case shows it in the data. - *The headline number is one of several.* The abstract's 3% matches the industry-adjusted figures (a 3.02% return spread and a 2.99% six-factor alpha). Announcement returns for high-IL firms are significantly negative in the two specifications without industry effects and insignificant with them. - *The predictive words are hard to read.* The LASSO's 149 selected terms include *infringement*, *product liability*, and *fraud*, and also *majeure*, *bailiff*, and *attornment*. The text describes a pre-2015 training sample and a post-2015 test sample but reports no out-of-sample fit. The authors do warn that a zero coefficient does not make a word uninformative. - *Some counts do not reconcile in the manuscript.* The text gives 112,716 firm-years and the descriptive table 112,457. The reputation sample is 11,329 in the text and 11,256 or 12,598 in the regressions. The final typeset version may resolve these. The lesson from @sec-sw-theory-building applies here too: every sample size in the prose should be recomputable from a table. None of this undoes the contribution. It marks what a successor paper can add, and the authors' own conclusion lists two of the items: more sources (earnings calls, social media, press coverage) and better language models. ### Carrying the template into a marketing journal Marketing is full of constructs that firms describe in words and no database records. A firm's exposure to a product-harm crisis, its dependence on a few customers or one retailer, its reliance on a celebrity or founder, its privacy and data-breach exposure, and the gap between its sustainability claims and its operations are all discussed in filings, earnings calls, complaints, and reviews, and none has a standard variable. One of the authors had already applied the recipe on the asset side, with a brand measure built from the frequency of the word *brand* in filings [@boustanifar2025brand] (@sec-branding). Seen together, the two papers are one research program: pick an off-balance-sheet quantity, find the text in which firms must discuss it, count, validate, and price. Four adjustments help a marketing version. - **Validate against people as well as outcomes.** Have trained coders rate a few hundred documents on the construct, report agreement among them, and report how the measure tracks their ratings. Predictive tests show that a measure is useful. Agreement with human judgment shows that it measures what its name says (@sec-reliability-validity). - **Tabulate the horse race.** Put the parent dictionary, a share-scaled version, an embedding-expanded dictionary (@sec-tad-culture-dictionary), and an LLM coder (@sec-llm-extraction) in one table with the same outcomes. If the simple count wins or ties, transparency is the argument for it. If it loses, the paper has a better measure. - **Choose outcomes a marketing reader prices.** Recalls, regulatory actions, complaint volume, brand-tracking scores, customer churn, and retailer delistings can play the role that class actions and RepRisk play here. Stock returns remain available for a strategy audience (@sec-marketing-finance). - **Decide what the last third of the paper is.** A finance paper ends with pricing. A marketing paper can end with a decision instead: which firms should change disclosure, product design, or claims, and what it is worth to them. If the measured facts raise a question that reduced-form evidence cannot settle, a small model is the other way to finish (@sec-sw-measure-model). ::: {.callout-tip} ## A checklist for the measurement paper 1. Name the construct by its relation to one the field already measures, and define it with a rule that says what is in and what is out. 2. Open with a named case in which the standard data record nothing and the stakes are plainly large. 3. Explain who produces the source text, under what obligation, and with what incentive to distort it. 4. Start from a published instrument. Document deletions and additions with examples, and print the full instrument in an appendix. 5. Estimate how the raw count scales with document length before choosing between a share and a controlled count, and say which results use which. 6. Show that the measure sorts known groups and finds known cases, then report how much variance those groups leave unexplained. 7. Predict future outcomes drawn from independent sources, across units and within unit. 8. Tie the measure to a price or a decision. 9. Put the nearest existing measures, and the parent instrument, in the same table. Report the top terms' share of the count and the measure recomputed without them. 10. Validate against human coding as well as against outcomes. 11. Show where in the source the signal sits and which terms carry it, with out-of-sample fit. 12. Print the raw descriptive pattern even when it runs against the conditional one, and make every sample size recomputable. ::: ## The Front End {#sec-sw-front-end} The front end—title, abstract, and introduction—is the part of the paper most people read and the only part most people read. It carries the entire promise– payoff loop of @fig-sw-paper-flow in compressed form, and a reviewer's accept-lean or reject-lean is often set before the methods section begins. The front end deserves a disproportionate share of writing effort precisely because it does a disproportionate share of the persuasive work. ### The title A title's job is to name the contribution in eight to fifteen words such that the right reader stops scrolling. It should contain the paper's key constructs (the terms a searcher would type) and, where possible, signal the relationship the paper establishes rather than merely the topic it addresses. "Brand Prominence and Status Signaling" names a topic; "Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of Brand Prominence" names a relationship and a mechanism. Question titles and two-part titles (a hook before the colon, the substance after) are common in JCR and JM and rarer in *Marketing Science*, reflecting the venues' different house voices—a difference worth matching to the target journal. ### The abstract The abstract is the most-read and least-revised 250 words in science, and the imbalance is a mistake. It must be **self-contained**: a reader who sees only the abstract should be able to state the paper's objective, method, principal finding, and implication. The canonical structure mirrors @eq-sw-chain in miniature—one or two sentences each for the problem, the approach, the result (with direction and, where it fits, magnitude), and the "so what". Two failure modes dominate. The **descriptive abstract** announces what the paper does ("we examine the effect of X on Y") without ever stating what it *found*, leaving the reader no wiser; the **overloaded abstract** crams in every robustness check and moderator, drowning the headline. The fix for both is the same: lead with the finding. ### The introduction as a funnel The introduction is where most rejections are decided, and it has a near-mechanical structure: a **funnel** from the broad problem to the specific contribution. A robust template runs problem $\rightarrow$ tension or puzzle $\rightarrow$ gap $\rightarrow$ "in this paper we" $\rightarrow$ approach $\rightarrow$ findings $\rightarrow$ contributions $\rightarrow$ roadmap. @fig-sw-funnel renders it. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-sw-funnel %%| fig-cap: "The introduction funnel.
